hook: Vinegar is an acid, but ethanol, which has the same O–H group, is not acidic enough to change pH at all. Swap one hydrogen in vinegar's acid for chlorine and the acid becomes about eighty times stronger. The reason sits in the structure of the ion left behind after the proton leaves.

prereq.why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of all elements (4.0).

prereq.q: What do the two resonance structures of the acetate ion, CH₃COO⁻, show?
options: The negative charge is shared between the two O atoms
The ion switches back and forth between two shapes
One O atom always carries the charge
The C atom carries the negative charge
prereq.why: Resonance structures describe one real ion in which the charge is delocalized over both O atoms.

prereq.q: HA has Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁴ and HB has Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁸. Which is the stronger acid?
prereq.why: A larger Ka means the acid ionizes more.

figure.caption: Each extra oxygen, or a more electronegative central atom, stabilizes the conjugate base and strengthens the acid.

chain.cause: An acid HA gives up H⁺ and leaves A⁻ behind
chain.effect: the more stable A⁻ is, the further HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ lies to the right

chain.cause: Electronegative atoms near the acidic group pull electron density toward themselves
chain.effect: the negative charge of A⁻ is less concentrated, so A⁻ is more stable and Ka is larger

chain.cause: Resonance spreads the charge of A⁻ over several atoms
chain.effect: carboxylic acids are far stronger than alcohols, and oxyacids with more O are stronger

chain.cause: Down a group, the bond to H gets longer and weaker
chain.effect: HF < HCl < HBr < HI and H₂O < H₂S < H₂Se in acid strength

chain.cause: An amine N has a lone pair
chain.effect: amines are weak bases that accept a proton on nitrogen

ideas: Acid strength follows conjugate base stability. Stabilize A⁻ and Ka goes up.
Oxyacids: more O atoms, or a more electronegative central atom, means a stronger acid (HOI < HOBr < HOCl < HOClO).
Carboxylic acids: the carboxylate is stabilized by resonance; electron-withdrawing groups (Cl, F) nearby make the acid stronger.
Binary acids: across a period electronegativity rules (CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF); down a group bond strength rules (HF < HCl < HBr < HI).
Amines (–NH₂) are weak bases: the proton goes on the N lone pair.

misconception.wrong: More hydrogen atoms in a formula make a stronger acid.
misconception.right: Only hydrogens that can leave as H⁺ count, and strength depends on how stable the conjugate base is. CH₄ has four H atoms and is not acidic; HCl has one and is strong.

summary: An acid is strong when the ion it leaves behind is stable. Electronegative atoms pull electron density from the acidic group, resonance spreads the charge of the conjugate base, and a large atom holds charge over a larger volume; each makes Ka larger. Amines are weak bases that accept a proton on the nitrogen lone pair.
